title: Integrated Population Balance and Multiphysics Modeling for Predicting Undesired Agglomeration in Small Molecule Manufacturing
authors: Prakitr Srisuma, Peter Hou, Shashank Venkat Muddu, Neda Nazemifard, Allan S. Myerson, Richard D. Braatz
abstract: Agitated filter dryers (AFDs) are a crucial unit operation in small molecule manufacturing that enables simultaneous filtration, washing, and drying of active pharmaceutical ingredients. One of the key challenges in AFDs is associated with undesired agglomeration, where the presence of hard agglomerates results in off-spec products, equipment damage, and additional downstream processing. This article presents a novel mechanistic model that describes the formation of soft and hard agglomerates during agitated filter drying. By integrating population balance and multiphysics modeling, the model can accurately predict the evolution of the product temperature, moisture content, and particle size distribution, and hence quantify the extend and impact of undesired agglomeration across various operating conditions. Our proposed model-based framework enables the rational design and operation of AFDs for improving the product quality and process reliability.
summary: This paper presents a comprehensive, integrated mechanistic model combining Population Balance Modeling (PBM) with multiphysics analysis to predict particle agglomeration in agitated filter dryers. By tracking soft and hard agglomerates, the model allows for the rational design and operation of pharmaceutical drying processes to ensure consistent product quality. This work is valuable for process engineering optimization in solid-state chemical manufacturing.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is predicting and mitigating undesired agglomeration of small molecules during the agitated filter drying (AFD) process, as hard agglomerates lead to off-spec products and equipment damage.
main_result: The developed model successfully predicts the evolution of particle size distribution (PSD) and quantifies the impact of agglomeration, showing that process parameters like solubility and mass transfer rates significantly influence the final particle size.
method: The authors developed a novel mechanistic model by integrating Population Balance Modeling (PBM) with multiphysics modeling to describe heat, mass, and particle dynamics.
model_or_system: The system is an Agitated Filter Dryer (AFD) used in pharmaceutical manufacturing. The model couples energy balance (heat transfer), mass transfer (solvent evaporation), and a PBE that explicitly tracks the formation and breakage of soft and hard agglomerates.
key_observables: Product temperature (T), moisture content ($m_l$), Particle Size Distribution (PSD), and the populations of soft ($\sigma$) and hard ($\eta$) agglomerates.
important_parameters: Solubility, mass transfer rates, and the ratio of liquid bridge disappearance to solid bridge formation are key parameters influencing agglomeration kinetics.
main_assumptions: The system is assumed to be well mixed due to continuous agitation, and the model makes specific functional form assumptions for the agglomeration and breakage kernels dependent on moisture content.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the AFD setup, the mechanistic model components, and time evolution plots showing mass, particle number, and PSD (D90/D99) under varying conditions, confirming mass conservation.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the industrial problem (agglomeration in AFDs) to presenting the integrated PBM/Multiphysics framework, detailing the governing equations for energy and mass transfer, and finally validating the model against experimental data and theoretical limits.
why_interesting: While the subject is chemical engineering, the rigorous application of population balance equations, coupled with complex transport phenomena modeling, shares mathematical parallels with kinetic rate processes studied in non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.
